title: PV^gamma = const holds for irreversible free expansion
statement: The polytropic relation P V^gamma = constant and T V^(gamma - 1) = constant applies to all adiabatic processes, including irreversible free expansion into a vacuum.
incorrect_statement: The polytropic relation P V^gamma = constant and T V^(gamma - 1) = constant applies to all adiabatic processes, including irreversible free expansion into a vacuum.
erroneous_reasoning: Students associate the equation $P V^\gamma = \text{constant}$ solely with the word 'adiabatic' ($dQ = 0$), neglecting the second essential prerequisite: that the process must also be quasi-static and reversible ($dS = 0$).
why_it_fails: The derivation of $P V^\gamma = \text{constant}$ integrates $dU = - P dV$, which requires well-defined equilibrium pressure throughout the gas and reversible boundary work. In free expansion against vacuum, $P_{\text{ext}} = 0$, so $W = 0$ and $\Delta U = 0$, resulting in constant temperature ($T_f = T_i$), in total contradiction to $P V^\gamma = \text{constant}$.
correct_physics_explanation:
The relation $P V^\gamma = \text{constant}$ is derived by combining the differential First Law $dQ = dU + P dV$ with $dQ = 0$, $dU = n C_V dT$, and the ideal gas equation $P = n R T / V$. This derivation strictly assumes that:
1. The process is reversible (quasi-static), ensuring the system passes through a continuum of thermodynamic equilibrium states with spatially uniform pressure $P$.
2. The mechanical work done by the system is given by the reversible boundary integral $W = \int P dV$.
In an irreversible free expansion (Joule expansion) of an ideal gas into an insulated evacuated vessel, the gas expands against zero opposing external pressure ($P_{\text{ext}} = 0$). Therefore, the work done on the surroundings is zero: $W = 0$. Because the container walls are thermally insulated, heat exchange is also zero: $Q = 0$. By the First Law of Thermodynamics:
$$\Delta U = Q - W = 0 - 0 = 0$$
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature ($U = U(T)$), which means $\Delta T = 0$, or $T_f = T_i$. The temperature does not drop at all! If one naively applied the reversible formula $T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}$, one would falsely predict a drastic temperature drop $T_f = T_i (V_i / V_f)^{\gamma - 1} < T_i$. Free expansion generates entropy ($\Delta S = n R \ln(V_f / V_i) > 0$), and applying $P V^\gamma = \text{constant}$ is completely physically invalid.
corrective_explanation:

refutation_counterexample: An insulated rigid box is divided into two equal compartments of volume $V$ by a thin partition. Compartment 1 contains $1\text{ mol}$ of an ideal gas ($\gamma = 1.4$) at $T_0 = 300\text{ K}$; compartment 2 is evacuated. The partition ruptures, and the gas freely expands into compartment 2, doubling its volume to $2V$. Since $Q = 0$ and $W = 0$, $\Delta U = 0 \implies T_f = T_0 = 300\text{ K}$. However, if $T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}$ were applied, it would predict $T_f = 300 \times (1/2)^{0.4} \approx 227\text{ K}$, an error of $73\text{ K}$ and a severe violation of energy conservation.
supporting_evidence: H.C. Verma, Concepts of Physics Vol 2, Chapter 27 (Specific Heats of Gases), Section 27.8: 'Free Expansion'; Fundamentals of Physics by Halliday, Resnick, Walker, Section 19-8; Question thermodynamics-question-3fe51020.
diagnostic_check_latex: \text{Free Expansion: } Q = 0, \; W = 0 \implies \Delta U = 0 \implies T_f = T_i \neq T_i \left(\frac{V_i}{V_f}\right)^{\gamma - 1}
diagnostic_symptom: Student applies T V^(gamma - 1) = const or P V^gamma = const to free expansion or sudden burst of a container into a vacuum.
